 Why every day should be a sunscreen day
 Sunscreen is one of the most important preventive measures in dermatology. Protecting the skin should become as routine as brushing one’s teeth.
 Pauline Songco · Nov 13, 2026, 2:32 AM
 DERMATOLOGISTS say sunscreen should be worn daily, not just during beach trips. — Photograph courtesy of Sarah Sheedy/unsplash 
 For many Filipinos, sunscreen is something that comes out only before a beach trip or a day spent under the sun. Dermatologists, however, say that mindset needs to change.
 Skin experts are encouraging people to make sunscreen part of their daily routine, pointing to the country’s tropical climate and consistently high ultraviolet (UV) index as reasons why sun protection should extend far beyond vacations and outdoor activities.
 During a recent skincare forum, dermatologists emphasized that the effects of UV exposure are cumulative. Even short periods under the sun while commuting, walking outdoors, driving, or sitting near windows can contribute to skin damage over time.
 REGULAR UV protection helps reduce the risk of sun damage, pigmentation and premature skin aging. — Photograph Courtesy of Crystal Weed/unsplash 
 Sunscreen is one of the most important preventive measures in dermatology. Protecting the skin should become as routine as brushing one’s teeth.
 Sunlight is among the leading environmental factors affecting skin health. Prolonged exposure to UV rays has been linked to premature skin aging, hyperpigmentation, uneven skin tone, and damage to the skin’s natural barrier. Over time, repeated exposure may also increase the risk of developing more serious skin conditions.
 The need for protection has become even more relevant as dermatologists observe a growing number of patients seeking treatment for concerns such as acne marks, melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and sun-related discoloration.
 These conditions, they explained, are often made worse by unprotected exposure to sunlight.
 Beyond the visible effects on the skin, experts also highlighted the emotional impact that skin conditions can have on people’s lives.
 In addition to applying sunscreen every morning, it is recommended to reapply it throughout the day when spending extended periods outdoors. Other protective habits include wearing wide-brimmed hats, sunglasses, long sleeves, and seeking shade whenever possible, particularly during peak sunlight hours.
 Sunscreen is not only for people with fair skin or those concerned about beauty. Regardless of skin tone, everyone can experience sun damage. While melanin offers some natural protection, it does not eliminate the harmful effects of UV radiation.
 The discussion also underscored how changing weather patterns, increasing heat, and environmental pollution continue to place additional stress on the skin. Combined with everyday UV exposure, these factors reinforce the importance of maintaining a simple but consistent skincare routine focused on prevention rather than correction.
 As more Filipinos become interested in skincare, dermatologists hope the conversation shifts beyond chasing trends or trying the latest products.
 Instead, they encourage people to focus on the basics — cleansing gently, moisturizing appropriately, and most importantly, wearing sunscreen every day.
 Because whether it’s a sunny afternoon, an overcast morning, or an ordinary commute to work, experts agree on one message: Every day is a sunscreen day.
